title: What is JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness): the standard tool for writing reliable JVM microbenchmarks that accounts for JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination, GC, and CPU scheduling: how do you set up a JMH benchmark (`@Benchmark`, `@State`, `@Setup`, `@Param`, `@Fork`, `@Warmup`, `@Measurement`, `@BenchmarkMode`), why must you return or consume computed values (blackhole) to prevent the JIT from eliminating dead code, and why is `System.nanoTime()` in a loop NOT a valid Java benchmark (no warm-up, no fork isolation, GC noise, dead-code elimination)?

s1_definition.oneliner: JMH is the correct way to benchmark JVM code because it handles warm-up, forking, GC, and dead-code elimination that a naive nanoTime loop gets catastrophically wrong.
s1_definition.profdef: JMH is the OpenJDK's official harness for writing trustworthy JVM microbenchmarks. It is built by the same people who build the JVM, and it exists because naively timing code with `System.nanoTime()` gives wrong numbers. JMH automatically handles JIT warm-up, runs in forked JVMs for isolation, measures across many iterations, and provides a Blackhole to consume results so the JIT cannot delete your code as dead. You annotate methods with `@Benchmark` and configure the run with annotations like `@State`, `@Setup`, `@Param`, `@Fork`, `@Warmup`, `@Measurement`, and `@BenchmarkMode`.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness)?

You write a benchmark by annotating a method with `@Benchmark`. JMH will call that method repeatedly and measure it. The `@BenchmarkMode` annotation chooses what to measure: `Throughput` (operations per second), `AverageTime` (average time per operation), `SampleTime` (a distribution including percentiles), or `SingleShotTime` (one call, for cold-start measurement). You usually report throughput or average time.

### How does JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) work?

State and setup are handled with `@State` and `@Setup`. A class marked `@State(Scope.Benchmark)` holds objects shared across threads, or `Scope.Thread` for per-thread state, and JMH injects it into your benchmark method. A method marked `@Setup` prepares that state before measurement, for example creating the accounts you will transfer between, so setup cost is not counted in the timing. `@TearDown` cleans up. `@Param` lets you run the same benchmark across several input values, like different transfer amounts or data sizes, and JMH runs every combination.

### Why does this matter?

The run is controlled by `@Fork`, `@Warmup`, and `@Measurement`. `@Fork` runs the benchmark in a fresh, separate JVM (often two or more forks), which isolates it from other code and averages out JVM-to-JVM variation from things like different compilation decisions. `@Warmup` specifies warm-up iterations that run but are not measured, giving the JIT time to compile the hot path to C2-optimized native code so you measure steady-state performance, not interpreted cold code. `@Measurement` specifies the real timed iterations.

### How do you use this in practice?

The Blackhole is critical. The JIT is aggressive: if you compute a value and never use it, the JIT proves the computation has no effect and deletes it entirely, which is dead-code elimination. Then your benchmark measures nothing and reports absurdly fast times. To prevent this, you either return the value from the `@Benchmark` method (JMH consumes returned values) or inject a `Blackhole` and call `blackhole.consume(value)`, which forces the JVM to treat the value as used. This is exactly why a hand-rolled nanoTime loop is invalid: it has no warm-up so it times interpreted code, no fork isolation so other code pollutes it, it includes GC and scheduling noise with no statistical treatment, and it is wide open to dead-code elimination and constant folding. A senior nuance: JMH also guards against loop optimizations and constant folding, reports variance across iterations so you can judge significance, and should be run on a quiet machine with other work stopped.

### What are the rules and constraints?

This aspect of JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) is important for banking applications at National Bank of India. Rajesh regularly considers this when designing transaction processing systems.
sections.s6_takeaway:
JMH, the Java Microbenchmark Harness, is the OpenJDK's official tool for writing trustworthy microbenchmarks, and it exists because benchmarking the JVM by hand almost always produces wrong numbers. You write a benchmark by annotating a method with at-Benchmark, and you configure the run with annotations: at-BenchmarkMode picks whether you measure throughput or average time, at-State and at-Setup provide and prepare fixtures outside the timed region, at-Param sweeps the benchmark across several input values, at-Fork runs each benchmark in a fresh isolated JVM, at-Warmup runs unmeasured iterations so the JIT has time to compile the hot path to optimized native code, and at-Measurement is the actual timed phase. JMH then aggregates across forks and iterations and reports an average with an error margin so you can tell whether a difference is real.

The single most important detail is consuming your results. The JIT is aggressive, and if you compute a value and never use it, the JIT proves the computation has no observable effect and deletes it entirely, which is dead-code elimination. Then your benchmark is timing nothing and reports impossibly fast numbers. JMH solves this by consuming any value you return from the benchmark method, or by giving you a Blackhole whose consume method forces the JVM to treat a value as genuinely used. This is exactly why a hand-written loop around System.nanoTime is not a valid benchmark: it has no warm-up so it times cold interpreted code, no fork isolation so other code pollutes the measurement, no statistical treatment of GC pauses and CPU scheduling noise, and it is wide open to dead-code elimination and constant folding, so the number it prints is essentially meaningless.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this came up when the team debated whether string concatenation was fast enough for building statement lines, and a colleague "proved" it was by timing a nanoTime loop whose result the JIT had quietly eliminated. I rewrote it as a proper JMH benchmark comparing concatenation against StringBuilder, parameterized by the number of statement lines, with warm-up, two forks, and a Blackhole consuming the results. The data was unambiguous: at a thousand lines StringBuilder was roughly forty times faster, because concatenation builds a new string every iteration. We switched to StringBuilder and wired the benchmark into our pipeline to catch future performance regressions on hot methods. The lesson I always repeat is that you never trust a benchmark that lacks warm-up, forking, and a Blackhole, because the JVM is far too clever to be measured naively.
